## What is the real challenge?

**LeetCode 146 — LRU Cache.** Implement an abstract data type that meets operational contracts and complexity targets.

This LeetCode label may describe a **problem domain, engineering interface or probabilistic method** rather than a universally named algorithm. The first step is to state which contract is required.

## The tempting solution

Keep cached keys in a plain array; find and move a key by scanning the whole array on every hit.

## The idea worth remembering

Design problems ask for a DATA-TYPE CONTRACT, not one magic algorithm. For LRU, a hash map plus doubly linked list supports lookup and recency updates without full scans.

## One mathematical expression — with every symbol explained

$$
S_{t+1}=Op(S_t,a_t)
$$

**Every symbol means:** S_t is the cache state before operation t; a_t is a get or put request; Op describes the state transition; S_(t+1) is the resulting cache and recency order.

**Numerical substitution:** Capacity 2: put(A,1) gives recency [A]; put(B,2) gives [B,A]. get(A) moves A to newest: [A,B]. put(C,3) evicts least-recently used B, leaving [C,A]. Every step follows the same state transition rules.

The substituted numbers are not decoration: if the example disagrees with the formula, the statement or its assumptions must be corrected before code is written.

## Why the method is justified

The list contains exactly one node for each key in the map. Its head/tail encode newest/oldest access. Moving a known node to the front and evicting the tail preserves these invariants.

**Complexity or resource cost:** Expected O(1) get/put using hash map plus linked list; O(capacity) memory.

## Executable example

The following small example can be run directly in its own environment:

~~~js
const cache=new Map(),capacity=2;
function put(k,v){ cache.delete(k); cache.set(k,v);
 if(cache.size>capacity) cache.delete(cache.keys().next().value); }
function get(k){if(!cache.has(k))return -1;
 const v=cache.get(k);cache.delete(k);cache.set(k,v);return v;}
put('A',1);put('B',2);get('A');put('C',3);
console.log([...cache.keys()]); // ['A','C'] oldest to newest
~~~

Run the JavaScript with Node.js; it illustrates the precise toy case from the formula.

## Which assumption makes it fail?

If you only use a Map but do not manage recency explicitly, you have no proven LRU contract. In languages with insertion-ordered maps you can use their semantics deliberately, but verify updates on get.

For this topic, distinguish an **exact probability or invariant** from a single random observation or a successful local test. A test samples executions; it is not a proof that all executions behave correctly.
